::: {.center}
# 1 Look {data-name="Look"}
:::

## 1.1 From a filter to a sequence logo

- `cutoff_for` → `windows_above` → `pwm_of` → logo: collect the windows with the highest output, count letters per position
- Logo height = information content: 2 bits = always the same letter, 0 = all four equally often

![](assets/custom/filter_logo.png){fig-align="center" height="492px"}

::: {.notes}
- Left: filter 0's 40 weights. Right: its logo, built from the roughly 25,000 windows in bound sequences whose output is above the cutoff (half-way between the filter's mean and maximum output). The notebook's count differs slightly because it scans a different subset.
- Information content at a position is 2 minus the entropy of the letter frequencies, in bits. Each letter's height is its frequency times that value.
- A logo shows which windows activate a filter. It leaves out the letters the filter penalises (its negative weights).
- TODO-1 builds a logo for every filter with these helpers, then `consensus_of` reads off the most frequent letter at each position.
:::

| Step | Task | Names | Time |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|

::: {.notes}
- The shuffle here reorders the motif's own letters. Slot 6 uses a stricter shuffle that keeps letter-pair counts.
- Expect a jump in the score once a copy lands near letter 175 (the fourth copy). The next two slides explain why.
:::

## 2.2 Insert the motif (TODO-2)

![](assets/custom/dose_response.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- 1,000 random RNA sequences. The dotted line is their mean score with nothing inserted.
- Insert the motif 1 to 7 times (black), the most that fit in a 330-letter sequence, and the same letters in shuffled order (grey). Compare the two curves rather than each curve with the baseline: the shuffled copy has the same letters, so it also changes the score.
- `plant()` writes copy n starting at letter 40 + 45(n − 1). The score jumps when copy 4 (letter 175) lands in the region the CNN weighs and falls again with more copies, as they replace more of the background.
:::

## 2.3 Position matters

![](assets/custom/position_scan.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- One copy of the motif at every position, averaged over 400 random sequences (a given cell in the notebook). The numbers 1 to 7 mark where `plant()` puts each copy in the previous test.
- The motif changes the score only between about letters 140 and 190, where almost every sequence in the data has its measured site (shaded).
- The shuffled copy gets much of the same increase there, so a good part of the effect is the letters' composition in that region rather than their order.
- This is the last-layer pattern from Slot 2: the CNN weighs positions. It reflects how the data were cut, and it means the answer to "does this motif matter?" depends on where it is placed.
:::

::: {.center}
# 3 Seed sites {data-name="Seed sites"}
:::

## 3.1 Does the CNN respond to seed sites?

![](assets/custom/planting_bars.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- The hypothesis from Slot 1: a model that learned AGO2 targeting should respond to seed sites. This is the bonus cell.
- 6 copies of each site inserted into real unbound sequences, against the same letters shuffled (grey: mean and standard deviation over 10 shuffles).
- miR-15/16 (UGCUGCU): 0.53 against 0.31 ± 0.09, a clear effect. miR-19, miR-30 and let-7 lie within the spread of their shuffles.
- The CNN was not given seed sites and responds to one of the four tested. The logos did not reveal this site; the insertion test did.
- Inside the 40-letter measured site, these seed sites are 3 to 6 times enriched in bound sequences but occur in only about 1 to 2% of them, so the signal is weak.
- The notebook's shuffle numbers differ slightly from these because the shuffles are random.

Next (Roee): models pretrained on the whole genome.
:::
